# Lincoln National Corporation (LNC) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-07-27. Price used throughout: $41.42 per share on the New York Stock Exchange (US dollars), a market value of about $7.9 billion. Transcripts reviewed: five consecutive quarterly earnings calls, 2025-05-08 through 2026-05-07.*

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Lincoln's story across these five calls is unusually consistent — which is itself the finding. Management has told the same three-part story every single quarter since early 2023, and the wording barely moves: fortify the capital base, make the operating model more efficient, and shift the business mix toward products that earn more per dollar of capital.

What *has* changed is the tense. In May 2025 the language was defensive and conditional: "the strategic actions we have taken over the past two years to fortify our foundation… better positioning us to manage through a period of market turbulence," with an explicit note that they were "holding a capital buffer as a proactive safeguard in the event of a market downturn." By the February 2026 call the same executive was describing "a more resilient capital foundation" and saying they "remain focused on continuing to improve returns on capital and to manage capital with greater flexibility over time." That is a shift from building a cushion to spending one — the single most important tonal move in the set.

Three growth drivers were introduced and stuck: (1) the Bain Capital partnership, announced roughly six weeks before the May 2025 call, which brought in $800 million of minority equity plus an asset-management relationship; (2) the Bermuda-based reinsurance subsidiary, which moved from "launched" in early 2025 to "over a year in the operational phase" by October 2025; and (3) a deliberate pivot inside annuities toward spread-based products — fixed annuities and registered index-linked annuities, where the company earns an investment margin rather than a fee on market value.

One driver was quietly reversed. Through 2025 management celebrated annuity sales growth — $3.8 billion in the first quarter of 2025, $4.5 billion by the third, full-year volumes up 25%. Then in February 2026 the CEO pre-announced that variable-annuity volumes in 2026 would be "intentionally lower and more closely aligned with pre-2025 levels." By May 2026 that had happened: variable-annuity sales of $1.4 billion were down year over year. This is not a failure — it is a deliberate trade of top line for lower market sensitivity — but an investor reading only the 2025 calls would have been surprised.

The other quiet expansion is the legacy life insurance block. In July 2025 the chief financial officer volunteered that any further external reinsurance would "really be focused on that… legacy life block." In February 2026 he confirmed 2026 and 2027 would bring "a number of different actions, some external, some internal." By May 2026 he was still describing it as work in progress. That thread runs straight into the Bloomberg report of 2026-07-13 that Lincoln is in advanced talks with Talcott Financial Group over roughly $5 billion of life reserves.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Seventh consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth" in adjusted operating income | Q1 2026 call, 2026-05-07 | Corroborated at every step: +14% (Q1 2025, excluding prior-year items), +32% (Q2 2025), fifth consecutive quarter (Q3 2025), +31% (Q4 2025), +16% (Q1 2026). Adjusted operating income available to common shareholders was $326 million in the first quarter of 2026 against $280 million a year earlier. The screener also records earnings beats in 7 of the last 7 quarters. | Holds |
| "Growing our franchise" | Every call | The top line does not grow. Revenue was $17.61 billion in 2021 and $18.21 billion in 2025 — about +1% in four years, with a three-year compound rate of −1.3%. Sales volumes grew; revenue did not. | Diverges — growth is mix and margin, not scale |
| "Our capital foundation remains strong" | Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 calls | Confirmed with a hard number: the CFO stated the year ended at a risk-based capital ratio of 439%, against a 400% target and a 20-point buffer, and said that figure excluded the remaining Bain proceeds. Leverage is described as at its long-term target. | Holds |
| A "track record of delivering results" | Q2 2025 onward | The adjusted line delivers; the reported line does not. Earnings per share ran 7.43 (2021), 7.78 (2022), −4.92 (2023), 18.41 (2024), 5.84 (2025). Book value per share has compounded at about −14% a year over five years. Whatever is being delivered, it has not yet compounded shareholder book value. | Diverges materially |
| Growing free cash flow, with subsidiary remittances rising from $845 million in 2025 to a $1.2–1.3 billion medium-term range | Q4 2025 call, 2026-02-12 (slide 18) | This is a promise, not a result. Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow in the screener data is $243 million against trailing diluted earnings per share of $8.85 — a cash-conversion ratio of roughly 0.14. Cash-flow statements for a life insurer are genuinely noisy, but a fourteen-cents-on-the-dollar conversion is the weakest link in the entire bull case. | Unproven |
| Group Protection is the standout — "record quarter for earnings and its highest-ever margin" | Q2 2025 call | True and visible: Group earnings of $112 million in the first quarter of 2026 against $101 million a year earlier, supplemental-health premium up 28%, local-market premium growth the strongest in nearly a decade. | Holds |
| Group results are sustainable | Implied throughout | Management said the opposite, plainly, in July 2025: "our recent results are tracking better than what the long-term averages would look like." The $104 million of favourable reserve remeasurement in that quarter is a direct consequence. The best-looking segment is explicitly running above its own long-run assumptions. | Self-flagged reversion risk |
| The Bain proceeds are being productively deployed | Q1 2026 call | Partly. The CFO described the fixed-annuity account-value growth as on pace and the legacy-life captive restructuring as done, but said the larger use — "either repositioning the life portfolio asset base or looking at an external risk transfer deal" — is still being worked through, more than a year after the money arrived. | Partly delivered |

Two data points in the screener file need correcting before anyone builds a valuation on them.

First, the recorded "net cash of $38.3 billion" is an artifact, not an asset. It comes from treating $44.7 billion of cash and short-term investments on the March 2026 balance sheet as corporate cash. For a life insurer, that money backs policyholder obligations; it is not distributable. Actual corporate cash and equivalents were $7.3 billion against total debt of $6.4 billion, so the company's own filed net-debt figure is roughly −$1.0 billion. Anyone adding $200 a share of "net cash" to this valuation would be off by two orders of magnitude.

Second, the Altman-Z solvency score of 0.1 (and the 0.13 quoted in the peer-comparison file) is a misapplied tool. That model was built for manufacturers and reads any balance sheet dominated by investment assets and policy reserves as distressed. Every large life insurer scores similarly. The real solvency read is the risk-based capital ratio of 439% against a 400% target — comfortable, and improving.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising, steadily and without a stumble.**

- *Q1 2025 (2025-05-08)* — Defensive. The call opens on macro: "Market volatility remains high, and the external backdrop remains uncertain." Capital is framed as a "cushion in the event of adverse economic conditions." The confidence claim is about surviving: "well prepared to fulfil our commitments to shareholders and policyholders despite the ongoing uncertainty."
- *Q2 2025 (2025-07-31)* — First real assertion. "Our momentum is building. Our track record is increasingly evident and we're excited about the path forward." Also the first appearance of the hedge that recurs in every subsequent call: "Results will not be linear."
- *Q3 2025 (2025-10-30)* — Offensive language arrives: "accelerate our strategic priorities," "durable earnings power and a clear path to building long-term shareholder value." The annual assumption review — the yearly re-examination of the estimates underpinning reserves, and historically the moment life insurers take their worst charges — produced "a small favorable impact." That is a meaningful non-event.
- *Q4 2025 (2026-02-12)* — Peak confidence, and the first multi-year numbers. Full-year adjusted operating income at "its highest level in four years." A medium-term outlook with an explicit remittance range. Language moves from holding capital to managing it "with greater flexibility."
- *Q1 2026 (2026-05-07)* — Confident but more granular, and notably willing to pre-announce bad optics: variable-annuity volumes down on purpose, one large group customer lost on price, annuity earnings carrying "the known headwinds we previously communicated."

Guidance has become *more* specific over time, not less — the opposite of what a deteriorating story produces. In May 2025 there were no forward numbers at all; by February 2026 there was a dated medium-term remittance range on a numbered slide. Management raised its own bar voluntarily.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High, on the measure they guide to. Unproven, on the measure that matters most.**

Tracked promise by promise:

- *Risk-based capital above a 400% target with a 20-point buffer* — promised May 2025, confirmed every quarter, and quantified at 439% for year-end 2025. Delivered.
- *Group Protection margin expansion over top-line growth* — promised repeatedly, and demonstrated in the hardest possible way: they let a large customer lapse rather than cut price, and said so on the call (May 2026).
- *Fourth-quarter disability loss ratio "slightly in line with third quarter to maybe up a little bit"* — given October 2025. The Group segment continued to grow earnings into 2026, so this was not a miss.
- *2026 variable-annuity volumes back toward pre-2025 levels* — guided February 2026, delivered by May 2026 with sales down year over year. An unusual case of a company guiding down and then hitting it.
- *Fixed annuities as the growth runway* — guided February 2026; first-quarter 2026 fixed indexed annuity sales rose over 90% year over year, though total fixed annuity sales of $716 million fell as they walked away from price-competitive multi-year guaranteed products. Half-delivered, and honestly explained.

The 7-of-7 earnings beat rate in the screener fits this pattern. Beating every quarter for seven quarters is usually a sandbagging tell, and there is a mild version of it here: the recurring "results will not be linear" line sets a low bar that the adjusted operating line then clears. But the beats are corroborated by segment detail rather than by one-off items, so this reads as conservative framing rather than manufactured performance.

The unproven promise is the important one. The entire investment case rests on converting adjusted operating income into cash at the holding company — the $845 million to $1.2–1.3 billion remittance step-up. That was guided in February 2026 and has not yet been demonstrated in a single reported period. When pressed on what drives a near-50% jump, the CFO answered with process ("as the free cash flow continues to be robust, you would expect us to move that to the holding company") rather than components. And he explicitly excluded the one action that would most obviously fund it: "to the degree that we, for example, look at another external risk transfer deal, that would not be what is implied in the remittances."

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The legacy life block — asked three times, answered never.** In July 2025 Alex Scott of Barclays asked directly what an external reinsurance deal might look like. The reply: "it's too early for us to really talk about anything we're focused on there with real detail. We're studying all of the possibilities." In February 2026 Suneet Kamath of Jefferies asked whether the remittance guidance contained any such lever; the answer was no. In May 2026 the CFO was still describing it as under study. Bloomberg reported on 2026-07-13 that Lincoln was in advanced talks with Talcott Financial Group over roughly $5 billion of universal life reserves with secondary guarantees. The analysts were pushing on exactly the right thread for a full year, and management gave them nothing — which is defensible while a transaction is live, but means the market has been valuing this business without knowing its largest pending change.

**The remittance step-up.** Kamath, February 2026: "it is a pretty big jump from the $845 million you did in 2025… can you unpack what would lead to close to a 50% jump?" The response named the buckets (legacy life, operating model, capital allocation) but no magnitudes. This is the single largest unbridged gap between what management asserts and what an outside analyst can verify.

**Group disability durability.** Tom Gallagher of Evercore pressed in October 2025 on whether higher severity was noise or trend. The CFO drew a firm line — "I wouldn't really call the severity impact the trend. It was 1 month" — while conceding half the loss-ratio move was trend. Management is asking to be judged on the favourable half of a mix it has already said runs above long-run assumptions.

**Competitive pricing, raised by a rival.** In May 2026 Gallagher relayed Apollo's complaint about "irrational competition in the annuity market coming from incumbent insurers." The CEO conceded that certain product pockets — multi-year guaranteed annuities, and increasingly registered index-linked annuities — are "a pure price competition play," and that Lincoln has pulled back. Honest, but it concedes that pricing power is thinnest in the fastest-growing part of the product set.

**What analysts are not asking about, and should be.** Nobody on these calls pressed on the gap between reported results and adjusted results. In the first quarter of 2026 Lincoln reported a net loss available to common shareholders of $211 million, or $1.10 a share, alongside adjusted operating income of $326 million, or $1.66 a share — a $537 million divergence in a single quarter. That gap is mostly non-economic mark-to-market noise on hedges and guarantees, which is precisely why it is excluded, but it has been persistently large and persistently negative, and it is the mechanism by which book value per share has fallen while adjusted earnings have risen.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- *The reported-versus-adjusted gap is large and one-directional.* A $537 million divergence in the first quarter of 2026 alone; reported earnings per share of 5.84 in 2025 against roughly 7.90 on the adjusted basis. Consistently unfavourable non-operating items are not noise, they are a pattern.
- *Book value per share has compounded at about −14% a year over five years* while management describes a strengthening franchise. Some of that is the accumulated-other-comprehensive-income mark on the bond portfolio, which reverses as bonds pull to par — but not all of it.
- *The best segment runs above its own assumptions, by management's own admission* (Q2 2025). Group Protection is carrying the improvement narrative and is the segment most exposed to reversion.
- *The largest profit pool is shrinking.* Annuities earned $275 million in the first quarter of 2026, down 5% year over year, against $112 million from Group, $43 million from Retirement Plan Services and $41 million from Life. The three growing segments together are smaller than the one that is not.
- *Insiders are not buying.* Open-market activity shows a single purchase of 300 shares against five sales totalling 54,569 shares. After a run of this size, that absence of conviction is worth noting.
- *Cash conversion is weak.* Trailing free cash flow of $243 million against roughly $1.7 billion of trailing net income.

**Green flags**

- *Seven consecutive quarters of year-over-year adjusted operating income growth, and seven consecutive earnings beats* — corroborated segment by segment, not by one-off items.
- *Capital is genuinely rebuilt.* Risk-based capital of 439% at year-end 2025 against a 400% target, stated on the call, and stated as excluding the undeployed Bain proceeds. Leverage at its long-term target.
- *The worst business stopped bleeding.* Life Insurance earned $41 million in the first quarter of 2026, a $57 million year-over-year swing from a loss.
- *The mix shift is real and measurable.* Spread-based products were 64% of annuity sales in the first quarter of 2026; the company exited its external flow reinsurance treaty and now retains 100% of fixed-annuity sales, keeping the investment margin in-house.
- *Discipline is demonstrated, not just claimed.* Walking away from a large group customer on price, and pre-announcing a deliberate variable-annuity volume decline, are both costly signals that management means what it says about profitability over volume.
- *The annual assumption review passed cleanly* in October 2025 — "a small favorable impact." For a company whose 2023 loss was driven by exactly this exercise, an uneventful review is a real green flag.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary moved from defence to offence, then to moat.** "Fortify," "buffer," "cushion" and "safeguard" dominate the May 2025 call. By February 2026 the operative words are "flexibility," "deploy" and — appearing for the first time in the set — "broaden our strategic moat." Management only starts talking about moats when it believes the survival question is settled.

**Two personnel changes matter more than they look.** The investor-relations lead changed between the October 2025 and February 2026 calls (Tina Madon to John Muething). More significantly, in June 2026 Lincoln promoted Paul Spurr to chief risk officer and chief actuary. A new chief actuary arriving immediately before a multi-billion-dollar legacy-block risk transfer is a detail to file, not to over-read — but the person who signs off on the reserves being transferred is newly in the seat.

**"Balancing profitability, capital efficiency and lower market sensitivity" replaced "profitable growth."** The three-word formula in the 2026 calls contains no growth term at all. That is the most honest thing in the transcripts: this is a margin-and-capital story, not a growth story, and management has stopped implying otherwise.

**The medium-term outlook was a deliberate cost increase.** Putting a numbered remittance range on a slide in February 2026, after three years of refusing forward numbers, raises the penalty for missing. Companies do that when they are confident — or when they need the market to underwrite something.

**Retirement Plan Services keeps getting explained rather than fixed.** Stable-value outflows have been described as a headwind on every call in the set, with new products and "moderation" cited each time. Earnings grew 26% in the first quarter of 2026, so it is working, but this is the segment where the narrative has stayed constant the longest without a clean resolution.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: Strengthening.**

Every measurable capital indicator has improved across these five quarters: adjusted operating income up seven straight quarters, risk-based capital at 439% against a 400% target, leverage at its long-term target, the worst segment back to profitability, and a genuine shift toward products that earn a spread rather than a market-linked fee. Management has been specific, has raised its own bar voluntarily, and has taken visible short-term costs — a lapsed large customer, deliberately lower variable-annuity volumes — to prove the discipline is real.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing:** the entire re-rating case turns on converting adjusted operating income into holding-company cash, and that conversion is guided but not yet demonstrated. Lincoln has promised subsidiary remittances rising from $845 million in 2025 to $1.2–1.3 billion, explicitly *without* counting a legacy-block reinsurance transaction. If the cash arrives, the discount to peers closes. If it does not — if it turns out that the operating earnings are real but trapped in the operating subsidiaries — then this is a company that earns well on paper and compounds nothing for shareholders, which is exactly what the five-year book-value record already shows. Everything else in the file is second-order to that question, and the first hard evidence lands with second-quarter results on 2026-07-30.

**Economic moat: narrow, and stable.** The moat type is a combination of distribution scale and regulatory licence, with genuine switching costs on the in-force book — policyholders rarely move a life policy or an annuity once written, and Lincoln's advisor and workplace distribution relationships are decades deep and expensive to replicate. But the evidence caps the width. Management concedes that the fastest-growing product lines are "a pure price competition play," and the company competes by adding features rather than by charging more. The returns picture is mixed rather than eroding: return on equity of about 16.9% flatters a book value that shrank to get there, while Group Protection margins are genuinely expanding (record margins, 120 basis points of expansion in early 2025) and annuity earnings are declining by design. That combination — one line widening, one narrowing on purpose, capital ratios rising — reads as stable, not eroding.

**Secular threat: manageable.** There is no structural force melting the terminal value of US life insurance and retirement income. The demographics run the other way: an ageing population converting savings into guaranteed income is a growing addressable market, and Lincoln's registered index-linked and fixed indexed annuity products sit directly in it. The real risks here are cyclical and idiosyncratic — a credit cycle hitting the general account, an equity drawdown hitting variable-annuity account values and hedge costs, and the long tail of legacy universal-life guarantees written decades ago. Those are underwriting and balance-sheet risks, not disruption risks. The cheapness is therefore best read as a persistent risk discount on a legacy block that management is actively trying to sell, not as a structurally shrinking base — a fear-print with a real, nameable fear attached to it, rather than a value trap.
